lines.text: Nine o'clock. Before any real work, you type the same three prompts into three agents.
Check last night's errors. Fix the build that broke at two. Tell docs and mobile what billing changed. You are the scheduler, and the messenger.
Agent R Q runs that for you: tasks on a schedule, events that hand work from one agent to the next, webhooks that let GitHub start the work, and workflows that chain it all.
A prompt you type every morning is a prompt you forget on a busy one. And then nobody reads the errors.
Here, Ada starts a new task in storefront: read last night's error log, and open a task for every new error.
The calendar sets how it runs: once, or repeated. She picks Daily, at nine. Custom picks the days, such as weekdays only.
The footer shows the schedule as a cron line, and how long until it runs next.
Scheduled lists them all, from every workspace, each with its next run.
Open one to see its runs. Each run is a normal task for the agent, with its own thread and timeline.
And runs never pile up. While the last one is still waiting or in progress, the next one is skipped.
Agents can schedule work too. The billing agent sets itself a monthly check of unpaid invoices, over M C P.
Billing changed the invoice A P I. Now you tell docs. Then you tell mobile. Every change, you carry the news by hand.
An event is a named signal. Ada creates A P I changed, with payload guidelines: which endpoint, and what changed in it.
Triggers subscribe workspaces to it. When it fires, docs gets a task to update the A P I reference, and mobile one to update its client.
The instructions take the event's payload, so each task says exactly what changed.
Billing's task ends with that event. When its agent is done, it publishes it, with what changed and a short F A Q.
Docs and mobile get their tasks at once, and the event's page lists every task it started.
A trigger can fire its own event when its task is done, so one change can run down a chain.
C I went red at two in the morning. Nobody saw it until nine, and then someone still had to read the log.
Hooks turn requests from outside into events. Ada registers GitHub, and pastes its payload U R L into the repository's webhook settings.
Routes map GitHub's signals to her events: a failed build on the main branch fires C I failed.
So when the build breaks, the storefront agent gets a task with the failure in it, before anyone wakes up.
Every request is kept under Deliveries. Failed ones are retried, and you can replay one by hand.
Events work one hop at a time. But a release touches three workspaces. Where do you see the whole chain?
A workflow names it. Ada creates release pipeline, starting from the release ready event.
In the graph, drag a workspace onto an event to subscribe it, and an event onto a workspace to fire it when that task is done.
Billing deploys first, and fires deployed. Then docs writes the release notes and mobile points the app at the new A P I, side by side.
The same pipeline reads as text too: an indented outline you can review at a glance.
It warns you about steps that nothing reaches, and about dead ends.
To run it, give a task the workflow as its on completion step. When that task is done, the whole pipeline runs, one step after another.
Each step lands as a task in its own workspace, and the workflow lists every task it started.
Put that first task on a schedule, and the whole release runs every Friday.
But work that starts itself should still answer to you.
Any step can go to a person instead of an agent: set its responsibility to human.
Yolo is off unless you turn it on, so automated tasks still ask before they run a command.
Edit a schedule or delete it from its row. The runs it already made stay where they are.
Tasks on a schedule, events between agents, webhooks from GitHub, and workflows for the whole release. You set it up once.
What would you automate first? Tell us in the comments, and try it at Agent R Q dot com.
